This essay has no such process. It is a first-person account of the 1933 Simele massacre and Seyfo, and it closes on remembrance that is 'incomplete, constrained by the stories that were never told ... and the justice that remains unresolved.' Nothing is being resolved. Accepting it risks teaching the scorer to suppress memorialisation and Indigenous-rights coverage.
